diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Diagnosis

The fitness dropped from 3.133 to 0.979 when the body switched from the `bits.OnesCount64` ladder to the SWAR loop. The SWAR version expands each word into about 12 SSA arithmetic instructions (shifts, masks, adds, and a multiply), while `bits.OnesCount64` is a single operation in the SSA interpreter. The cost metric counts executed SSA instructions, so the SWAR expansion is far more expensive per word. The best-scoring programs all use one `OnesCount64` call per word.

## Change

Replace the SWAR inner loop with an 8-wide loop that calls `bits.OnesCount64` once per word. This restores the cheap per-word cost, keeps the loop overhead low (one branch and one reslice per 8 words), and removes the unused SWAR constants. The tail, which already uses direct `OnesCount64` calls, stays as it is.

## Expected effect

Each word now costs one `OnesCount64` instead of about 12 arithmetic SSA ops. The loop should cost roughly as much as the ladder per word, with lower overhead than the 16-word recursive version. Correctness is unchanged, since the arithmetic is the same popcount, and `xs` is still not modified because only the local slice header is resliced.

If this does not reach the 3.133 level, the next step is to return to the 16-word unrolled block with recursion (the best-scoring program), since it had the lowest per-word overhead measured so far.
